questions.stem: An archive job runs `for (Path p : reports) pages += Files.lines(p).filter(l -> l.startsWith("\f")).count();` over 6,000 reports, in a process allowed 4,096 open files. Nothing else in the process opens files. What happens?

options.text: It can fail partway, since a stream's file is released only once it is closed or garbage collected
options.says: without close() each stream holds its descriptor until a garbage collection happens to release it, so the job fails if none runs in time

options.text: It can fail partway, since a stream's file is released only once its pipeline has read the last line
options.says: if the last line released the file, count() would release each one and the job would finish; in fact only close() or a collection does

options.text: It finishes, since a stream's file is released as soon as its pipeline has read the last line
options.says: a terminal operation finishes the pipeline but releases nothing; only close() does

options.text: It finishes, since a stream's file is released as soon as it is closed or garbage collected
options.says: nothing closes these streams, and a collection runs when the JVM decides: in the page's run 981 of 1,000 leaked descriptors were still open after the loop

origin.section: A Stream Over a File Holds It Open Until close(), Not Until the Terminal Operation

questions.stem: A cache keeps its keys in a `HashSet<String>`, and its status page shows `keys.stream().findFirst()` labelled "oldest key". In a test, the keys user-17, user-42, user-58, user-63, user-71 and user-90 are added in that order, and the page shows user-17. Then 40 more keys are added and removed again. Can the page now show a key other than user-17?

options.text: No, since the stream order follows the order in which the keys were first added
options.says: a HashSet keeps no insertion order; that is LinkedHashSet

options.text: No, since the stream order follows the keys' hash codes, and those have not changed
options.says: the bucket layout depends on the table size too, and resizing for the extra keys can move the keys (a run showed user-63)

options.text: Yes, since the stream order follows the order in which keys were last added or removed
options.says: a HashSet records no history of additions or removals; its order is the bucket layout

options.text: Yes, since the stream order follows the table's bucket layout, and that has changed
options.says: a HashSet has no encounter order; its stream follows the bucket layout, which the resize changed

origin.section: A Collection's Stream Has the Collection's Order, and a HashSet Has None

questions.stem: A firewall check reads `int[] blocked = {21, 23, 445};` and then `boolean deny = Stream.of(blocked).anyMatch(p -> p.equals(port));` for a connection with `int port = 23`. What happens?

options.text: deny is true, since Stream.of spreads the int array into a stream of its three ports
options.says: an int[] is not a T[], so Stream.of(blocked) is a stream of one element, the array

options.text: deny is false, since Stream.of makes a stream of one element, the int array itself
options.says: Stream.of(blocked) is a Stream<int[]> of one element; p.equals(23) compares an array with an Integer

options.text: It doesn't compile, since p is an int there and an int has no equals method to call
options.says: p is the int[] itself, an object, so p.equals(port) compiles

options.text: It doesn't compile, since Stream.of accepts arrays of objects only, never an int array
options.says: Stream.of(T t) accepts the int[] as one object, so it compiles and runs

origin.section: Stream.of Streams Its Arguments: an int[] Is One Element, and So Is null

questions.stem: A test helper runs `Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 3).filter(n -> n < 500).forEach(System.out::println);`. It prints 1, 3, 9, 27, 81 and 243. What happens next?

options.text: It keeps printing, since filter never ends the stream and products that overflow can pass it
options.says: the two-argument iterate is endless, and once the products wrap, negative values pass n < 500

options.text: It keeps printing, since iterate restarts the stream from 1 once a product would overflow
options.says: iterate never restarts; it keeps applying n * 3 to the wrapped values

options.text: It stops after 243, since filter ends the stream at the first product of 500 or more
options.says: a filter drops elements but never ends a stream

options.text: It stops after 243, since iterate ends the stream once the next product would overflow
options.says: int multiplication wraps silently and the two-argument iterate never ends

origin.section: A Generated Sequence Ends Only Where Its Factory Says

questions.stem: An export joins the rows of 100,000 pages with `rows = Stream.concat(rows, page.rows().stream());` in a loop, starting from `Stream.empty()`, then calls `rows.toList()`. The JVM runs with default settings. What happens?

options.text: It returns every row, since each concat only wraps the stream before it and copies nothing
options.says: the wrapping is the problem: in the page's run, 50,000 nested concats overflowed the stack inside concat

options.text: It returns every row, since each concat copies both inputs into one flat stream
options.says: concat is lazy and copies nothing; each call wraps the previous stream

options.text: It throws an Error, since each concat wraps the stream before it, nesting 100,000 deep
options.says: each concat wraps the previous one; the page's run overflowed the stack (StackOverflowError) at 50,000

options.text: It throws an Error, since each concat copies both inputs, holding every row 100,000 times
options.says: concat copies nothing; the failure is the depth of the nesting, not memory

origin.section: Builder and concat Assemble a Stream; Repeated concat Overflows the Stack
